comparison: Both support localization findings (C1, C2, C5-C8). OpenEval emphasizes immunofluorescence data showing reduced colocalization and EEA1 puncta. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of 'convincing evidence' for the overall mechanism. OpenEval also covers C3, C4, C9 which peer reviewers address separately in R2.

OpenEval R1 includes C3, C4, C9 about endosomal disruption and early endosome formation. Peer R2 accepts these findings, with the editor noting TMEM127 loss 'inhibits endocytosis of a variety of cell surface receptors,' implicitly accepting endosomal disruption data.

Both support RET accumulation findings (C10-C16). OpenEval cites immunoblotting, surface biotinylation, and qRT-PCR data. Peer reviewers explicitly accept that 'deletion of TMEM127 causes RET protein accumulation on the cell surface' with 'compelling cellular and biochemical evidence.' Peer R3 also includes C110 about plasma membrane accumulation.

Both support broader membrane protein accumulation (C17-C18). OpenEval cites Figure 2—figure supplement 1D showing multiple proteins affected. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a strength, noting 'deletion of TMEM127 affected multiple classes of transmembrane proteins...suggesting a global effect.' Peer R4 includes additional claims C43-C45 about global effects.

Perfect alignment on internalization findings (C19-C26). Both support biotinylation internalization and recycling assays showing impaired GDNF-responsive internalization. OpenEval emphasizes time-dependent data; peer reviewers accept 'compelling cellular and biochemical evidence on how TMEM127 deficiency reduces RET internalization and degradation.'

Both support RET-clathrin colocalization findings (C28-C33). OpenEval cites TIRFM data showing differential patterns; peer reviewers accept without challenge, with editor noting paper demonstrates TMEM127 loss 'alters clathrin assembly.'

Perfect alignment on CCP formation findings (C34-C40). Both support multiple imaging modalities showing impaired CCP formation and reduced size. OpenEval emphasizes convergent data from TIRFM, epifluorescence, and SIM; peer reviewers describe biochemical analysis as 'thorough and impressive.'

OpenEval R7 addresses global membrane protein accumulation (C41-C48) with TIRFM and biotinylation data. Peer R4 covers overlapping claims C43-C45 and explicitly acknowledges this as a strength, noting the 'global effect on cell surface proteins' helps 'explain how TMEM127 mutations act as drivers in PCC as well as in other cancers.'

OpenEval R7 includes C46-C48 about global effects on membrane trafficking. Peer R16 addresses C46-C48, C116 about global effects, explicitly acknowledging this as a strength that helps explain TMEM127's role across cancer types.

Perfect alignment on CCP dynamics (C49-C54). Both support live-cell TIRFM data showing increased sCLS nucleation, decreased CCP initiation, and altered maturation. OpenEval emphasizes automated tracking; peer reviewers accept as part of 'convincing evidence' for altered clathrin assembly.

Perfect alignment on membrane protein mobility (C55-C59). Both support single-particle tracking showing altered EGFR diffusion. OpenEval emphasizes altered membrane dynamics; peer reviewers accept, with editor noting paper shows TMEM127 loss 'causes disorganization of plasma membrane lipid domains.'

Strong alignment on adaptor protein interactions (C61-C73). OpenEval supports proximity ligation assay data showing maintained but altered protein-protein interactions. Peer reviewers accept without challenge as part of overall mechanism supporting membrane-level defects. OpenEval also includes C60 not in peer result.

Perfect alignment on lipid raft organization (C74-C77). Both support immunofluorescence data showing altered lipid raft organization. OpenEval emphasizes global membrane defect; peer reviewers explicitly accept, with editor stating paper provides 'convincing evidence' for 'disorganization of plasma membrane lipid domains.'

Strong alignment on RET degradation (C79-C82). Both support cycloheximide chase data showing differential degradation kinetics. OpenEval emphasizes increased RET half-life; peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge 'compelling cellular and biochemical evidence on how TMEM127 deficiency reduces RET internalization and degradation.' OpenEval also includes C78 not in peer result.

Strong alignment on constitutive signaling (C84-C91). Both support immunoblot data showing constitutive RET phosphorylation and downstream signaling. OpenEval emphasizes ligand-independent signaling; peer reviewers accept that 'deletion of TMEM127 causes RET protein accumulation...and, thereby, increased its constitutive ligand-independent activity.' OpenEval also includes C83, C89 not in peer result.

OpenEval R13 supports ligand-independent signaling claims. Peer R15 questions this interpretation, with one reviewer requesting authors 'tune down their "ligand independent" claim,' suggesting the activity may be related to 'level of RET expression/strength of clustering' rather than true ligand independence. This represents a key disagreement.

Strong alignment on proliferation findings (C93-C100). Both support MTT assay data showing increased proliferation and RET inhibitor sensitivity. OpenEval emphasizes therapeutic implications; peer reviewers accept findings as 'nicely explained the mechanistic link between TMEM127 and tumorigenesis.' OpenEval also includes C92, C98 not in peer result.

OpenEval R15 includes background claims C106-C107 about TMEM127 and RET in PCC, supported by literature citations and experimental data. Peer R1 accepts these as part of the overall mechanism without challenge.

OpenEval R15 includes C108-C109 about endosomal defects, supported by literature and experimental data. Peer R2 accepts these findings as part of the mechanism, with editor noting TMEM127 loss 'inhibits endocytosis.'

Both support major conclusions (C112-C118). OpenEval cites comprehensive experimental data supporting the model. Peer reviewers provide strong endorsement, with editor stating paper provides 'convincing evidence' and reviewers describing 'novel mechanisms and key insights' into pheochromocytoma pathogenesis. OpenEval includes additional claims C110-C111, C119 not in peer result.

OpenEval R16 includes C110 about plasma membrane accumulation as a major conclusion. Peer R3 accepts this finding, with reviewers noting 'deletion of TMEM127 causes RET protein accumulation on the cell surface' with compelling evidence.

OpenEval R16 includes C111 about ligand-independent signaling as a major conclusion and rates it SUPPORTED. Peer R15 rates this UNCERTAIN, with reviewer requesting authors 'tune down their "ligand independent" claim,' suggesting it may reflect receptor density rather than true ligand independence. Key disagreement.

OpenEval supports C139 about mTOR activation being downstream of RET, citing immunoblot data and xenograft studies. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, noting a previous paper showed TMEM127 recruits NEDD4 for RET ubiquitination and requesting discussion of 'relevance between these two potentially different mechanisms (clathrin-mediated or ubiquitin-mediated).'

OpenEval R18 includes C140-C141 about mTOR signaling and therapeutic implications. Peer R19 accepts the supporting evidence, with editor acknowledging results are 'significant for understanding how RET127 loss contributes to pheochromocytoma' and reviewers noting immunohistochemical data from TMEM127-mutant PCC. Peer R19 also addresses C135 about PCC context.

Both rate extrapolations to other cancer types (C144-C149) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes claims are 'largely speculative extrapolations' lacking 'direct experimental validation in these other cancer contexts.' Peer reviewers request 'more discussion that why the loss of TMEM127 is more linked to the development of PCC compared to other cancer types.' Strong agreement on uncertainty. OpenEval also covers C142-C143 not in peer result.

Both rate context-dependent TMEM127 effects (C155-C157) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes claims are 'speculative extrapolations' requiring 'additional experimental validation across multiple systems.' Peer reviewers note TMEM127 has been 'linked to enhanced MHC-I-mediated tumor immunity' and request discussion of 'dual effects of TMEM127 in tumor control in the context of immunity.' Strong agreement on need for more discussion. OpenEval also covers C150-C154, C158-C159 not in peer result.

OpenEval supports background claims C119-C138 as accurately representing established literature with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background claims.
